paragraphs.heading: What a subgroup is
paragraphs.text: A subgroup of a group G is a subset whose members form a group using the same operation as G. We write H ≤ G to say that H is a subgroup of G. A proper subgroup is one that is not all of G, and it is written H < G. When H is a subgroup of G, G is sometimes called an overgroup of H.

paragraphs.heading: Testing for a subgroup
paragraphs.text: A subset H is a subgroup exactly when it is nonempty and closed under products and inverses. Closed under products means that for any a and b in H, the product ab is also in H. Closed under inverses means that a⁻¹ is in H whenever a is. The two rules can be merged into one, that ab⁻¹ lies in H for all a and b in H, though checking them separately is usually just as easy. If H is finite, being nonempty and closed under products is already enough.

paragraphs.heading: Shared identity, shared inverses
paragraphs.text: A subgroup has the same identity element as the whole group. Inverses also carry over: the inverse of an element inside H is its inverse in G too. Where two subgroups overlap, the overlap is again a subgroup, and the same holds for any collection of subgroups. For instance, in R² under addition, the x-axis and the y-axis meet only in the trivial subgroup.

paragraphs.heading: Subgroups built from elements
paragraphs.text: For any subset S of G there is a smallest subgroup that contains S, called the subgroup generated by S and written ⟨S⟩. Its elements are exactly the finite products of members of S and their inverses, with repeats allowed. A single element a generates a cyclic subgroup ⟨a⟩. If ⟨a⟩ is isomorphic to Z/nZ, then n is the least positive integer with aⁿ = e, and this n is the order of a. If ⟨a⟩ is isomorphic to Z, then a has infinite order.

paragraphs.heading: Cosets and counting
paragraphs.text: Multiplying all of H by a fixed element a gives a left coset, written aH. Every element of G lies in exactly one left coset of H. How many left cosets there are is called the index of H in G, written [G : H]. One result of this counting is that the order of every subgroup, and of every element, must divide the order of G.

paragraphs.heading: Normal subgroups
paragraphs.text: A subgroup H is called normal when aH = Ha holds for every a in G. Every subgroup of index 2 is normal, because its left cosets and its right cosets are just the subgroup and its complement. For example, the alternating group A₄, made of all the even permutations in S₄, has index 2 and so is normal.

paragraphs.heading: Symmetries of a square
paragraphs.text: The group S₄ has three subgroups with 8 elements each. Every one of them is isomorphic to D₄, the dihedral group made of the symmetries of a square. Number the corners of a square 1, 2, 3, 4 going clockwise, and each symmetry becomes a permutation of the labels. One such subgroup is generated by the quarter turn clockwise, (1234), and the flip across the diagonal through corners 1 and 3, which is (24). The three subgroups come from the three ways of choosing which numbers sit on opposite corners.
